scope: Minjerribah / North Stradbroke Island and the immediately surrounding Quandamooka (Moreton Bay) waters.
country_note: Minjerribah is Quandamooka Country. Nothing in this pack speaks for Quandamooka people. Species names here are English common names and scientific binomials only. No language words are used, because none could be sourced to a published, citable authority within this pass. Anything cultural belongs in data/lore.json, not here.

confidence_scale.high: Stated in a government, park authority or peer-reviewed source, or directly observable and uncontroversial.
confidence_scale.medium: Stated in a credible secondary source, or a government source read at one remove, or a figure that is dated and may have moved.
confidence_scale.low: Plausible and useful for simulation, but not verified for this island. Treat as a placeholder a local can correct.

native_species_recorded_diwa_wetland.note: Counts are for the North Stradbroke Island DIWA nationally important wetland boundary, which includes surrounding bay waters. That is why whales, seals and offshore dolphins appear in the mammal count.

island_context.joint_management: Naree Budjong Djara National Park is jointly managed by the Quandamooka Yoolooburrabee Aboriginal Corporation (QYAC) and the Queensland Parks and Wildlife Service.

habitats.name: Wallum heath and low woodland
habitats.description: Fire-adapted shrubland and low woodland on infertile Pleistocene sand. Wallum banksia over sedges, tea-tree and paperbark. Covers much of the island interior.

water_chemistry.note: Acid, tannin-stained, nutrient-poor. This is what makes the acid frogs possible and keeps most competitors out.

coverage_share_estimate.basis: Modelled placeholder for the sim. Not a mapped figure.

habitats.name: High dune eucalypt open forest
habitats.description: Tall open forest on the high dunes. Scribbly gum dominant, with blackbutt, pink and red bloodwood and blue gum, over a grass and shrub understorey. The most widespread forest on the island.

habitats.name: Eighteen Mile Swamp
habitats.description: Coastal freshwater swamp running behind the eastern ocean dune for most of the island's length. Sedge and paperbark, permanently to seasonally wet, fed by the water table not by runoff.

centroid.note: Approximate centroid of a long linear feature. Reconcile with data/geography.json.

superlative_claim.claim: Described in some sources as the largest coastal freshwater swamp of its kind.
superlative_claim.note: Superlative not independently checked. Do not put it in player-facing copy without a better source.

habitats.name: Freshwater lakes and lagoons
habitats.description: Over 100 freshwater lakes and wetlands. Two mechanisms, and they behave differently: window lakes sit in a hollow that intersects the regional water table, perched lakes sit above it on a sealed layer of organic matter.

members.name: Blue Lake (Karboora)
members.note: A window into the island's water table, so its level tracks the aquifer rather than recent rain. Culturally significant to Quandamooka people. Access is by the walking track from the park road.

members.name: Brown Lake (Bummiera)
members.note: Perched on organic matter above the water table. Tea-coloured from tannins. Culturally significant.

members.name: The Keyholes
members.type: lake chain at the northern end of Eighteen Mile Swamp

habitats.name: Acid ephemeral wetland and sedge swamp
habitats.description: Shallow, seasonally wet, low-pH sedge and reed beds inside the wallum. The breeding habitat that the acid frogs depend on and almost nothing else can use.

habitats.name: Littoral rainforest and spring-fed wetland (Myora)
habitats.description: Small pocket of closed forest and wetland on the western shore around Myora Springs (Capembah Creek), where fresh groundwater surfaces and runs to the bay.

spring_flow_litres_per_day.note: Single secondary source. Worth a local check.

habitats.name: Foredune and dune spinifex
habitats.description: The seaward face of the ocean dune. Beach spinifex sends runners across bare sand, traps windblown grains and builds the dune back after a storm. It is the island's cheapest coastal defence and the first thing foot traffic destroys.
habitats.sim_role: Erosion buffer whose strength scales with vegetation cover. Cover falls with unmanaged access tracks and rises with fencing, matting and planting.
habitats.source: general knowledge; supported by the dune-care material in C:/Users/sbt41/githublocal/grain-by-grain/shoreline.html

habitats.name: Ocean surf beach
habitats.description: Main Beach, Frenchman's, Cylinder, Home Beach and the long eastern strand. Pipi beds in the swash zone, gutters that hold tailor, sporadic turtle nesting above the high tide line.

habitats.name: Rocky headland and gorge
habitats.description: Point Lookout headland, North Gorge, Adder Rock. Deep water close inshore, which is why whales, turtles, manta rays and dolphins can be watched from land here.

habitats.name: Offshore rocky reef
habitats.description: Flat Rock, Shag Rock and the Manta Bommie complex off Point Lookout. Rocky outcrops in roughly 3 to 30 m, cleaning stations, sandy gutters.

members.name: Flat Rock
members.protection: Marine national park (green) zone since the 2009 Moreton Bay Marine Park rezoning. No fishing, no anchoring. Four permanent moorings installed 2012.

habitats.name: Eastern Banks seagrass meadow
habitats.description: The shallow sand banks west and north of the island: Amity, Wanga-Wallen, Moreton and Maroom Banks. Six main seagrass species. This is the dugong larder and it is why dugong are here at all.

habitats.name: Western intertidal sand and mud flat
habitats.description: The bay-side flats that drain at low tide off Dunwich, Amity and the northern banks. Feeding ground for migratory shorebirds, and the yabby and worm banks locals pump for bait.
habitats.sim_role: Feeding window is tide-driven. Bird energy intake only accrues while the flat is exposed; roost pressure only bites at high tide.

habitats.name: Mangrove and saltmarsh fringe
habitats.description: Western and southern shoreline fringe. Roots hold mud, take the punch out of a surge, and act as a nursery for young fish, prawns and crabs.
habitats.sim_role: Shoreline protection coefficient and a fish-recruitment multiplier for the bay fishery.

habitats.name: Deep bay channel
habitats.description: Rainbow Channel between Minjerribah and Mulgumpin (Moreton Island), and the deeper water off Amity. Fast-moving, deep, and the reason both the erosion problem and the shark history sit at Amity Point.

habitats.name: Township and garden interface
habitats.description: Dunwich, Amity Point and Point Lookout, their yards, verges and the road corridors between them. Where koalas meet cars and dogs, where possums get into roofs, and where most wildlife calls come from.
habitats.sim_role: The conflict layer. Nearly every negative wildlife event in the sim should originate here or on the roads.

habitats.name: Rehabilitating mineral sand mine site
habitats.description: Former mineral sand mining areas in the island interior, under progressive rehabilitation. Structurally young vegetation, different fire and fauna behaviour to intact wallum.
habitats.note: Sand mining on the island has ended; the Enterprise mine closed in 2019. Exact site boundaries and rehabilitation status belong in the geography and civic packs, not here.

population_estimate.basis: No published island-wide total was found. A 2019 University of the Sunshine Coast survey spotted 33 koalas over two days at selected sites, and drone thermal surveys were run for Redland City Council in 2020, but the reports are not publicly readable. The range is a modelling placeholder, not a count.

island_traits.isolation: Separated from the mainland population for roughly 8,000 years.
island_traits.genetics: Lowest genetic diversity of the south-east Queensland populations, consistent with long isolation.
island_traits.disease: Chlamydia is present but clinical disease is reported at lower rates than in stressed mainland populations. Lower habitat disturbance is the usual explanation offered. Do not describe this population as chlamydia-free.
island_traits.source: Cristescu, Ellis et al. (2012), 'North Stradbroke Island: an island ark for Queensland's koala population?', Proceedings of the Royal Society of Queensland; https://www.researchgate.net/publication/233810684

species.seasonal_note: Peak is the breeding and dispersal season through late winter and spring, when males move and vehicle strike and dog attack risk rise. Summer heat suppresses daytime movement.
what_disturbs_it: vehicle strike on the township roads and the Dunwich to Point Lookout road
habitat clearing and fragmentation in the township interface
what_helps_it: lower speed limits and driver warnings at dusk and dawn
keeping and replanting food trees on private land
cool patchwork burns that do not scorch canopy
species.sim_role: Flagship stewardship species. Slow-moving population under a road-and-dog mortality tax. Player levers: speed limits, dog rules, vegetation retention, fire regime. Second-order consequence: a speed limit that saves koalas also lengthens the ferry run to Point Lookout and annoys visitors.

population_estimate.basis: No island count located. Widely seen on the golf course, road verges and open ground near Dunwich and Amity.

species.seasonal_note: Crepuscular year round; more roadside grazing through the cooler, drier months when green pick concentrates on mown verges.
what_disturbs_it: vehicle strike at dawn and dusk
people approaching mobs, especially with food
what_helps_it: mown open ground away from roads
driver awareness signage on the main road
species.sim_role: Ambient population that produces road-strike events and the joey-in-pouch rescue case. Density responds to grassland area and rainfall.

population_estimate.basis: No island count located.

species.seasonal_note: Breeds year round; activity is more about cover and moonlight than season.
what_disturbs_it: vehicle strike on tracks and the main road at night
loss of dense understorey after hot fire
what_helps_it: unburnt refuge patches inside a burn mosaic
species.sim_role: Understorey-dependent browser. Population is a readout on whether the fire mosaic is leaving unburnt refuges.

status.note: Not listed, but the Moreton Bay islands population is a southern relict, isolated from the main range which now begins near Rockhampton. Its interest is biogeographic, not statutory.

population_estimate.basis: Described as rare and elusive on the island. No count located.

species.sim_role: Rare sighting event. A player who sees one should be told why it matters: it is evidence of how long these animals have been cut off from the mainland.

population_estimate.basis: Described as widely distributed on the island. No count located.

species.seasonal_note: Breeding season through winter brings echidna trains and daytime road crossings. In summer they shift activity to night and dusk to avoid heat.
what_disturbs_it: vehicle strike, worst in the winter breeding months
being picked up or relocated by well-meaning people
what_helps_it: being left exactly where it is
unsealed verges it can dig into
species.sim_role: Seasonal road-strike spike in winter. Also the rescue case where the correct player action is to record the location precisely and do nothing else.

population_estimate.basis: Described as widely distributed. No count located.

species.seasonal_note: Two loose breeding peaks, autumn and spring, which is when orphaned young turn up in rescue calls.
what_disturbs_it: cats and dogs, and a cat-caught possum is urgent even when it looks unhurt
roof exclusion done without a nest box replacement
what_helps_it: nest boxes where hollows have been lost
species.sim_role: Township nuisance-and-care species. Generates roof complaints and the commonest night-time rescue case.

population_estimate.basis: Reported present but uncommon on the island by a local tourism source. It did not appear in the DETSI native mammal list read for the North Stradbroke Island DIWA wetland, so presence is not confirmed by a government dataset in this pass.

species.verification_flag: Presence on the island needs local confirmation before this species is shown to players.
what_disturbs_it: loss of dense mid-storey and vine tangle
species.sim_role: Low-frequency sighting and rescue case. Flagged, not featured, until a local confirms it.

population_estimate.basis: Named as a species benefiting from the island fox and cat control program. No count located.

species.seasonal_note: More visible in winter when banksia and eucalypt nectar flows.
what_disturbs_it: gaps in the canopy wider than a glide
species.sim_role: Canopy-connectivity indicator. If the player fragments forest, gliders drop out before anything more visible does.

population_estimate.basis: Described as widely distributed. Named as a beneficiary of fox and cat control.

species.seasonal_note: Breeding peaks in the warm wet months. The conical nose-holes in lawns are the sign most residents notice.
what_disturbs_it: loss of dense ground cover to hot fire or clearing
species.sim_role: The clearest single readout of feral predator pressure. Bandicoot density should visibly track the fox and cat control budget.

population_estimate.basis: Cryptic and rarely seen. Rated a biologically important island vertebrate. No count located.

what_disturbs_it: nest mound damage from vehicles and foot traffic
sea level rise squeezing the saltmarsh band
what_helps_it: intact mangrove and saltmarsh with room to retreat inland
species.sim_role: The quiet listed species most players will never see. Its trend is a scoring input that only shows up in the stewardship readout, not on screen.

population_estimate.basis: Highly mobile, follows nectar flows across the region. Island numbers are a flow, not a stock.

species.seasonal_note: Numbers follow eucalypt and banksia flowering. Winter banksia flowering pulls them in.
what_disturbs_it: backyard fruit netting that is not wildlife-safe
species.sim_role: Pollinator and long-distance seed disperser: raises regeneration rates across the forest habitats. Also the one rescue path that is always a human-health emergency and must never be handled by a member of the public.
species.safety_rule: Never touch a bat, even to help, even if it looks dead. Vaccinated rescuers only. A scratch or bite means wash thoroughly and get urgent medical care.

population_estimate.basis: There is no established dingo population on Minjerribah. Local sources cite the absence of large predators as an island characteristic, in contrast to K'gari. A dingo record appears in the DETSI wildlife dataset for the North Stradbroke Island DIWA wetland, which may reflect a historic or boundary record rather than a resident population.

species.sim_role: Deliberate absence. The ecological gap a dingo would fill is instead occupied by roaming domestic dogs and, until recently, foxes. Do not put dingoes in the world. If a player asks why there are none, that is the answer.

population_estimate.basis: No count located. Commonly seen around campgrounds and picnic areas.

species.seasonal_note: Strongly seasonal. Largely inactive through the cold months, then very visible around campgrounds and bins through summer.
what_disturbs_it: being cornered or fed at campgrounds
species.sim_role: Campground and picnic-area presence that makes the island read as alive. Also a cane toad casualty: a rising toad population should visibly cost goannas.

population_estimate.basis: No count located.

species.seasonal_note: Spring is peak: males move to find mates and cross roads and lawns doing it.
what_disturbs_it: whipper-snippers and mowers in long grass
what_helps_it: a check of long grass before mowing
rock and log shelter left in yards
species.sim_role: Township species with its own rescue tile so it is never reported as a snake. Its trend responds to garden chemical use.

population_estimate.basis: No count located.

species.seasonal_note: Spring and early summer is when call volume spikes. Winter is close to silent.
what_disturbs_it: being approached or photographed close up
rodent bait, which poisons the snake through its prey
species.sim_role: Seasonal call-volume driver for the wildlife response system. Safety rule in the sim mirrors the real triage: an unidentified snake is treated as venomous, and the app never rewards moving closer.

population_estimate.basis: No count located.

what_helps_it: being left alone in a roof or garden
species.sim_role: Non-venomous counterweight in the snake call tree, and a free rodent-control service in the townships. Killing pythons should measurably raise the rat problem.

population_estimate.basis: Moreton Bay holds a resident feeding population of green turtles of all size classes. Nesting on Minjerribah is rare: a green turtle has nested repeatedly on the island, which is itself unusual. The bay is a feeding ground first and a rookery a distant second.

species.seasonal_note: Present year round on the seagrass. Nesting and hatching activity is a summer window, roughly December to March.
what_disturbs_it: boat strike in the shallow banks
fishing line, hooks and net entanglement
what_helps_it: fox control on the ocean beaches
lights off near nesting beaches in summer
no line or net left in the water
species.sim_role: Seagrass-linked grazer. Nesting is a rare, high-value event the player can protect or lose. The marine stranding hotline path is 1300 130 372.

population_estimate.unit: nests recorded on the island's ocean beaches, 2017/18 season
population_estimate.basis: Nest count for one season, not a population. Loggerheads nest sporadically on Moreton, North Stradbroke and South Stradbroke Islands.

species.seasonal_note: In south-east Queensland mating starts about late October and peaks in December. Females come ashore roughly December to February and may nest up to four times in a season. Nesting finishes late February or early March.
what_disturbs_it: fox predation of nests and hatchlings
vehicles compacting nests on the ocean beach
what_helps_it: sustained fox control, which is why the last recorded nest predation on the island was in late 2016
lights off and a clear run to the water for hatchlings
vehicle exclusion above the high tide line in nesting season
no hooks pulled by members of the public
species.sim_role: The highest-stakes seasonal ecological event on the ocean side. A single summer of lapsed fox control should be visible in the next season's hatchling number.

population_estimate.basis: No island estimate located. Calling-male counts at known sites are the usual survey unit.

species.seasonal_note: Calling and breeding follow warm-season rain filling the sedge beds.
what_disturbs_it: trampling of reed beds where lake visitation is high, named as a real problem on North Stradbroke Island
drainage and lowering of the water table
any change that raises water pH toward neutral, which lets predatory fish and competing frogs in
what_helps_it: boardwalks and defined tracks at popular lakes
keeping the water acid and the swamp undrained
groundwater extraction held below the level that drops perched wetlands
species.sim_role: The wallum's canary and the sharpest test of a water-versus-visitors trade-off. Its population should respond to the groundwater system and to visitor numbers at lake sites, not to rainfall alone.

population_estimate.basis: No island estimate located.

species.seasonal_note: Unlike most local frogs this one calls strongly through the cooler months, so the wallum has a winter frog chorus. Calling follows rain more than temperature.
what_helps_it: fire that does not burn out the peat
species.sim_role: Winter audio layer for the wallum at night, and a second, differently-timed acid-wetland indicator so the player cannot read the whole system off one species.

population_estimate.basis: No island estimate located.

species.sim_role: Third acid frog, giving the wallum an audible community rather than one flagship.

population_estimate.basis: Listed in the DETSI wildlife dataset as a distinct North Stradbroke Island population. Taxonomy unresolved.

species.sim_role: An island-specific form. Worth surfacing to the player as a reason this island is not interchangeable with any other sand island.

population_estimate.basis: Moreton Bay regularly supports more than 1 per cent of the flyway population. This is a bay-wide figure; the island's western flats are one part of it.

species.seasonal_note: Non-breeding summer visitor from the northern hemisphere. Arrives from about August and September, peaks over the southern summer, departs by about March and April. A small number of immature birds over-winter.
what_disturbs_it: people and dogs walking through a high-tide roost
drones, to which this species is exceptionally sensitive at all distances and altitudes tested
loss of roost sites to development and sea level rise
habitat loss on the flyway, especially the Yellow Sea staging grounds, which is beyond any island lever
what_helps_it: roost buffers, with a drone exclusion of about 475 m around waterbird flocks recommended in the literature
dogs on lead or excluded from roost beaches
signage and volunteer roost wardens over the summer
intertidal flats kept free of vehicles
species.sim_role: The clearest disturbance mechanic in the pack. Every roost flush costs an energy budget the bird has to make back before it can fly to Russia. Player levers are dog rules, drone rules and roost signage; the flyway itself is outside the player's control, which is an honest and useful limit to model.

flyway_share.basis: The Ramsar Information Sheet for Moreton Bay, published 1 December 2023, records the site as regularly supporting 9.02 per cent of the flyway population against the Hansen et al. 2016 estimate of 35,000 birds, and 9.87 per cent against the Wetlands International 2008 estimate of 32,000. This is a bay figure, not an island one.
flyway_share.why_it_matters: About one bird in eleven of the entire East Asian-Australasian Flyway population of this species spends the southern summer in this bay. That is the number that makes a roost on these flats a matter for four countries rather than for a council.

instruments.note: It is on the EPBC Act migratory species list because it is on those instruments: a bird on an annex to the three bilateral agreements, or on Appendix I or II of the Bonn Convention, must be placed on that list. None of the instruments prohibits disturbing it. What they oblige is habitat conservation, cooperation and, in the Bonn Convention, a prohibition on taking, which means killing or capturing and not flushing. See data/civic.json treaty_layer.

species.seasonal_note: Non-breeding summer visitor. The baueri subspecies makes the direct trans-Pacific flight from Alaska, which is why pre-departure fat gain in March matters so much.
what_helps_it: the same dog and drone rules that protect the curlew
species.sim_role: Second flyway species, so the shorebird system does not rest on one bird. Also the one to use when explaining to a player why a five-minute disturbance can matter to an animal on a schedule.

flyway_share.basis: The Ramsar Information Sheet for Moreton Bay, published 1 December 2023, records the site as regularly supporting 3.59 per cent of the flyway population of Limosa lapponica. A bay figure, not an island one, and recorded at species level rather than by subspecies.

instruments.note: The Ramsar Information Sheet lists this species as migratory under CMS as well as the three bilateral agreements. The Convention's own species page for Limosa lapponica shows no appendix listing, and this pack does not resolve the two against each other: the three bilateral agreements are recorded because both sources agree on them, and no CMS appendix is asserted. See data/civic.json treaty_layer.

population_estimate.basis: No island or bay figure captured in this pass.

species.sim_role: Small-bodied member of the mixed roost flock. Included so the flock is a community rather than two named birds.

population_estimate.basis: No island figure captured in this pass.

species.sim_role: Mixed roost flock member.

population_estimate.basis: Resident and scarce. No island figure located.

species.seasonal_note: Resident, unlike the migrants. Nests on open beach in the warmer months, which puts eggs directly in the path of dogs and vehicles.
species.sim_role: Resident shorebird, so the player cannot dismiss the shorebird system as a summer-only problem.
Visible resident on the flats. Its pairs are territorial and stable, so a player can watch the same pair across years.

species.seasonal_note: Nests on open sand in the warm months, which is exactly when the beaches are busiest.
what_disturbs_it: beach traffic and dogs at nesting sandspits
species.sim_role: Ties the shorebird system directly to summer visitor numbers.

population_estimate.unit: breeding pairs on and around the island
population_estimate.basis: Territorial and long-lived; a handful of pairs is plausible for an island this size but no count was located.

species.seasonal_note: Breeds through the cooler months, roughly winter into early spring. Pairs are visible over the headlands and the bay year round.
what_disturbs_it: loss of tall shoreline nest trees
what_helps_it: drones kept away from nests and roosts
species.sim_role: Apex bird. Its presence over a beach or the bay is a cheap, strong signal that the place is alive. Nest sites are point features a player can protect or lose.

species.seasonal_note: Autumn to spring breeding. Ospreys readily nest on poles and towers as well as dead trees, so infrastructure choices matter to them.
what_disturbs_it: fishing line ending up in nests
what_helps_it: artificial nest platforms where natural trees are gone
line bins at jetties and boat ramps
species.sim_role: The species that shows infrastructure and wildlife are not always opposed: an osprey platform on a pole is a cheap, visible player action with a fast payoff.
Mangrove-linked raptor. Its presence over the western shore is a mangrove-condition signal.

population_estimate.basis: No island count located. Usually seen in pairs, trios or small groups rather than flocks.

species.food_dependency: Feeds almost exclusively on Allocasuarina and Casuarina seed cones. It also needs large hollows to nest in, so it depends on two slow-growing resources at once.
what_disturbs_it: fire that kills stands of she-oak, since the trees take years to bear cones again
clearing of she-oak on private land, which is easy to mistake for scrub
what_helps_it: she-oak stands protected from repeat fire
she-oak planted as part of any revegetation
species.sim_role: The species that makes fire frequency legible. Burn the same block twice too close together and the she-oak seed crop, and the cockatoos, do not come back for years. This is the second-order consequence the fire system needs.

species.seasonal_note: Spring and summer breeder that nests in a tunnel dug into bare sandy ground, including track edges and sand cuttings. Many birds move north for winter.
what_disturbs_it: vehicles and foot traffic over nest burrows in sandy banks and track edges
sand bank works during the breeding season
what_helps_it: sandy banks and track cuttings left undisturbed from about September to January
species.sim_role: A ground-nesting bird whose nests are in exactly the places people drive. Good for teaching that a track alignment decision is an ecological decision.

status.epbc: Not listed as threatened; removed from the threatened list in 2022. Still protected as a listed migratory species and a cetacean under the EPBC Act.

population_estimate.basis: A 2022 figure of as many as 40,000 and a preliminary 2024 report of more than 50,000. Growth of about 10 to 11 per cent a year over the past decade. Use the range, not a single number.

species.seasonal_note: Northward migration roughly June to August, southward roughly September to November. The southward leg brings cows with calves closer inshore, which is why late-season watching from the Point Lookout headland is often the best. Peak months as modelled here: July north, October south.

viewing.best_from_land: Point Lookout headland and the North Gorge walk
viewing.why: Deep water sits unusually close to the headland, so whales pass within sight of the cliff.

what_disturbs_it: vessels approaching inside the legal distance
entanglement in fishing and shark control gear
what_helps_it: gear retrieved and not left in the water
land-based viewing promoted over close boat approach
species.sim_role: The seasonal tourism engine and the clearest calendar event in the whole simulation. Whale season drives visitor numbers, ferry loads, accommodation prices and headland crowding, which then feed back into shorebird disturbance and parking. Also carries the entanglement incident.

status.epbc: Not listed as threatened; protected as a cetacean

species.seasonal_note: Resident in Moreton Bay all year round. Regularly seen from the Amity Point jetty and off Point Lookout.
what_disturbs_it: feeding by people, which teaches dependence
what_helps_it: net and line kept out of the water
species.sim_role: Everyday marine presence that makes the bay read as inhabited. Visible from the jetty, so it is one of the few marine species a walking player meets without a boat.

cultural_reference.summary: Quandamooka people had a cooperative fishing relationship with dolphins in these waters, in which dolphins helped drive fish toward shore. Amity Point is named in the historical record for this. Welsby (1917) records that at Amity Point the animals were tame enough to be handled.
cultural_reference.handling_rule: This is cultural and historical material. It belongs in data/lore.json with its citation and a Traditional Owner review, not in this pack. It is noted here only so an ecology system does not silently contradict it. Do not render it in player-facing copy from this file.
cultural_reference.source: Welsby, T. (1917), cited in Wild Dolphin Provisioning at Tangalooma, Moreton Island: An Evaluation, https://www.tangalooma.com/TangaloomaV2/media/Documents/Dolphins/Wild-Dolphin-Provisioningat-Tangalooma-an-Evaluation.pdf

population_estimate.note: Earlier estimates from 1984 to 1987 gave 119 to 163. A small, fragmented population across roughly five social communities.

species.seasonal_note: Resident all year round. Much scarcer and shyer than the bottlenose, and easily confused with it at a distance.
what_disturbs_it: boat strike and traffic in shallow water
species.sim_role: Rare sighting worth much more than a bottlenose sighting. A population of about 128 in the whole bay means a handful of individuals matters; the sim should treat a single death as a significant event.

status.epbc: Listed migratory and marine; not listed as threatened nationally

seasonal_range.note: Within-year variation is large because animals move in and out of the bay.

species.distribution_note: More than 95 per cent of the bay's dugong occur on the Eastern Banks, off the island's western and northern side, where the water is clear, boat traffic is light and deep water is close by.

grazing_effect.note: Herds graze one location for weeks to months, then move on. The meadow recovers. This is a natural cycle, not damage, and a simulation should model recovery not just removal.

species.seasonal_note: Bay numbers are higher in summer and lower around July, based on the range across the aerial survey series.
what_disturbs_it: seagrass loss after flood plumes and turbidity
vessel traffic pushing animals off feeding banks at the wrong tide
what_helps_it: catchment water quality, which is largely a mainland lever not an island one
species.sim_role: The seagrass system's payoff animal, and the clearest demonstration that a decision made on the mainland can hurt the island. Model dugong numbers as a function of seagrass area and quality with a lag of seasons, not ticks.

population_estimate.unit: individuals visiting the Point Lookout cleaning stations
population_estimate.basis: Manta Bommie is described as a nationally significant gathering site, second to Lady Elliot Island. Photo-identification catalogues exist but no total was captured in this pass.

species.seasonal_note: Warm months. Commonly given as November to May, peaking over summer, at the cleaning station on the bommie.
what_disturbs_it: divers and snorkellers chasing or touching animals, which drives them off the cleaning station
what_helps_it: no touching or blocking the cleaning station
species.sim_role: Summer counterweight to the winter whale season, so the marine tourism economy has two peaks with different rules. Behaviour responds directly to diver conduct, which makes it a good lever for a player.

population_estimate.unit: individuals at the Flat Rock aggregation
population_estimate.basis: Flat Rock is one of three sites in Moreton Bay Marine Park identified as critical to the survival of the east coast population. Counts are made by divers through the aggregation season but no figure was captured in this pass.

aggregation_site.structure: Two sandy channels in the reef
aggregation_site.protection: Marine national park (green) zone since the 2009 rezoning: no fishing, no anchoring. Fishing prohibitions and diving restrictions at the critical habitats were introduced in December 2003. Four permanent moorings installed in 2012.

what_disturbs_it: divers crowding the gutters, especially blocking the exits
what_helps_it: diver group size and approach limits
species.sim_role: A protected aggregation the player can measurably help or harm through zone enforcement and dive management. It is docile despite its appearance, which is worth teaching.

species.seasonal_note: More active in warm water, and more so in turbid water after rain.

amity_point_history.summary: Amity Point sits beside the Rainbow Channel, a deep, fast-moving passage between Minjerribah and Mulgumpin. On 7 January 2006 Sarah Kate Whiley, aged 21, was fatally attacked by bull sharks while swimming there. Fish offal had been dumped in the water nearby. It was the first fatal attack at a beach carrying Queensland Shark Control Program gear since the program began in 1962.
amity_point_history.handling_rule: Treat this with the restraint owed to a death in a small community. Use it to explain why the channel is not a swimming beach and why offal disposal matters. Do not dramatise it, do not build a game event on it, and do not put a named person into the world.

what_helps_it: fish waste disposed of on land, not thrown off the jetty or the cleaning table into the water
species.sim_role: A real risk factor tied to a specific place and a specific human behaviour. The lever is fish waste handling and swimming location, not culling. The correct player action in a sighting is everyone out of the water calmly and alert the lifesavers.

status.note: Managed under Queensland fisheries rules with size and possession limits. Check current limits in the civic or economy pack rather than here.

species.seasonal_note: Winter into early spring, with August and September named as the strong months. Fish work the gutters along Main Beach and the ocean strand and through to Amity.
what_disturbs_it: beach vehicle pressure on the gutters
species.sim_role: Winter fishing economy and a reason for residents and visitors to be on the beach at dawn in the cold months. Ties the ocean beach to the household food and social calendar.

species.seasonal_note: The mullet run: schools leave the estuaries in winter to spawn and travel along the beaches in visible dark patches. Given as May to August on the island's beaches.
species.sim_role: The most visible seasonal ecological event on the beach and a long-standing food source. Feeds the tailor and the dolphins, so a mullet-run parameter should drive several other species at once. This is the right place to model an event a player can watch from the sand.

population_estimate.basis: No island survey located. Density is the meaningful unit; the banks are patchy.

species.seasonal_note: Pumped year round on a low tide; effort peaks with school holidays and the warm months.
what_disturbs_it: heavy pumping pressure on the same bank
species.sim_role: The bottom of the bait chain and a shared common. A good small-scale tragedy-of-the-commons model: one popular bank near the ramp gets hammered while others sit unused.

population_estimate.unit: individuals per square metre of swash zone

what_disturbs_it: vehicle traffic through the swash zone
what_helps_it: vehicle routes kept off the wet sand where beds sit
species.sim_role: Direct link between the beach driving policy and a living resource. It is also the food that makes the ocean beach worth foraging.

population_estimate.basis: Oyster leases exist in these waters. Location and area belong in the businesses or geography pack.

filtration_rate.value: about a bathtub of water per adult oyster per day
filtration_rate.note: A rule of thumb, useful for a plain-speech explanation rather than a precise model input.

species.seasonal_note: Growth and spat fall track water temperature, so the warm months do the work.
what_disturbs_it: poor water quality and flood plumes
historic dredging, which removed the bay's original reefs
what_helps_it: shellfish reef restoration where sea Country custodians agree to it
species.sim_role: Water quality made visible. Oyster condition is a slow, honest readout of what the catchment is doing, and shellfish reef restoration is a buildable player option that improves clarity, fish shelter and wave attenuation at once.
species.consent_note: Any reef or offshore sand placement in this simulation must be modelled as requiring Quandamooka agreement through QYAC, because that is the real constraint.

population_estimate.basis: Numbers have fallen sharply. The coordinated program reports removing about 90 per cent of the foxes over more than a decade of work; an older advocacy estimate put the island population between 1,000 and 2,000, which now reads as high and is best treated as historic. Redland City Council trapping on its own land removed 126 foxes and 10 feral cats from 2009.

control_program.best_timing: Denning and mating season, about April to June, continuing to about November.
control_program.outcome_marker: The last recorded turtle nest predation on the island was in late 2016.

what_helps_it: a break in control between seasons
species.sim_role: The single best demonstration in the pack that a small continuing budget beats a large occasional one. Control effort must be modelled as a rate, not a one-off purchase: stop for two seasons and the turtle nests, bandicoots and ground-nesting birds all go backwards at once. This is the island's clearest ecological success story and it is reversible.

population_estimate.basis: Harder to count and harder to remove than foxes. Council trapping on its own land removed 10 feral cats from 2009.

what_helps_it: unowned and semi-owned cats fed near townships
cats allowed to roam at night
species.sim_role: The harder half of the predator problem, and the one that runs through the townships rather than around them. Its lever is partly regulatory (registration, containment) and partly social, which makes it a good civic system input as well as an ecological one.

species.seasonal_note: Breeds through the warm wet months. Wet summers produce the big cohorts.
what_disturbs_it: tadpole trapping using chemical lures, which can take thousands of tadpoles from a waterbody in hours
acid wallum water, which limits where they can breed
what_helps_it: permanent neutral-pH water in gardens and dams
pet food and outdoor lights that concentrate insects
species.sim_role: Poisons goannas, blue-tongues and snakes that mouth them. The acid wallum wetlands are partly a natural barrier, which gives the player a reason to keep water acid rather than tidy. Community tadpole trapping is a C-hour style volunteer activity with a measurable result.

status.note: Managed under Redland City Council's animal management local law.

population_estimate.basis: Council registration data would give this. Not captured in this pass.

species.seasonal_note: Tracks holiday periods rather than weather. School holidays and long weekends bring visiting dogs as well as resident ones.
what_disturbs_it: trapping programs for dogs left to roam
what_helps_it: no consequence for off-lead beach use
species.sim_role: Third leg of the predator problem, and the only one the player can address purely through rules and persuasion. Dog attack is the third-ranked recorded koala mortality cause on this island, and the same dogs flush shorebird roosts and take bandicoots and wallabies. Model it as a per-household behaviour with a compliance rate, not as a pest population.

population_estimate.basis: Deer were not named in any island pest source read for this pack: not the Friends of Stradbroke Island pest page, not the national fox and cat project page, not the council material. Feral deer are a real problem elsewhere in south-east Queensland. Absence here is an absence of evidence, not a confirmed absence.

species.verification_flag: Ask a local or Council land management before either adding deer to the world or stating publicly that there are none.
species.sim_role: Not in the world. Retained as an explicit zero so a later agent does not add deer from mainland habit.

plants.role: Structural dominant of the wallum. Woody cones need fire to release seed. Winter flowering feeds gliders, flying-foxes and honeyeaters when little else is out.
plants.fire_response: Serotinous. Requires fire at an interval long enough for plants to build a seed store, and short enough to trigger release. Too-frequent fire empties the store.

plants.role: Dominant of the island's most widespread forest, regional ecosystem 12.2.6. Secondary koala food tree. The scribbles are the tunnels of a moth larva under the bark.
plants.fire_response: Resprouts from epicormic buds after fire.

plants.role: Tall forest tree on the high dunes. Hollow-bearing when old, so it carries gliders, possums and cockatoos.
Primary koala food tree, on the wetter ground. Winter nectar source for flying-foxes and lorikeets.
Koala food tree. Present in the high dune forest.
Dominant of the wet, poorly drained country. Its litter is part of what keeps the swamp water acid and tannin-stained.
Shrub layer of the heath. Contributes to water acidity and tannin colour.
Low spreading shrub of sandy soils and rainforest margins. Speckled white berry, sweet, ripening in summer and autumn. Grows wild on Cylinder headland.
plants.note: A well-documented bush food of this region. Any account of its use by Quandamooka people belongs in data/lore.json with a citable source, not here.

plants.role: Prop-rooted dune and headland tree. Holds the back dune, defines the look of the coastal edge, drops a large segmented fruit.
plants.threat_note: Pandanus dieback caused by the pandanus planthopper has affected trees along the south-east Queensland coast. Whether it is currently active on this island was not verified in this pass.

plants.role: Salt-tolerant dune tree. Litter suppresses understorey and the roots fix nitrogen in poor sand.
The glossy black-cockatoo's food tree. Cones take years to build a crop, which is why repeat fire in a she-oak stand removes the cockatoos for years afterwards.
Tall fan palm of moist gullies, swamp margins and littoral rainforest. A visual marker that the ground is wet.

The foredune builder. Runners spread across bare sand, trap windblown grains and rebuild the dune after a storm cuts it back. The seed head rolls along the beach in the wind. This plant is the island's cheapest coastal engineering and a single unmanaged access track will cut a line straight through it.

sim_parameter.effect: Multiplier on dune recovery rate after a storm cut, and on the volume of sand the foredune can hold.
sim_parameter.basis: Mechanism is well established; the coefficient is a modelling choice.

weeds.impact: Smothers native ground and shrub layer. Named as a widespread island problem.
Forms dense thickets behind the dune. Recorded behind Frenchman's Beach.
weeds.spread_vector: spread by rainbow lorikeets feeding on it

weeds.impact: Garden escape that establishes in bushland and on other trees.
Very hard to remove once established; deep taproot.
Toxic to stock and spreads from every dropped plantlet.
Serious dune weed elsewhere on this coast, listed for the island.
Bird-spread garden escape into closed forest.

weeds.common_name: Bitou bush, lantana and groundsel bush
weeds.scientific_name: Chrysanthemoides monilifera subsp. rotundata; Lantana camara; Baccharis halimifolia
weeds.impact: All three are significant weeds of coastal south-east Queensland: bitou on dunes, lantana in disturbed forest edges, groundsel on wet margins.
weeds.verification_flag: None of these three appeared on the Friends of Stradbroke Island weed list read for this pack. Their presence and severity on this island is unverified. Do not show them to a player until a local or Council land management confirms.
weeds.source: general knowledge; absence noted against https://fosi.org.au/backyard-bushcare/

processes.name: Fire regime
processes.summary: The wallum needs fire and is damaged by too much of it. The island's management now combines traditional fire practice led by QYAC with modern hazard reduction, coordinated across Council, the fire service, Seqwater, QYAC and Queensland Parks.

reference_event.name: 2013 to 2014 bushfires
reference_event.evacuations: residents plus more than 900 campers and their vehicles

cultural_burning.summary: Large old cypress pine trees on the island indicate a long history of cultural burning with mild fires, and their survival depends on that practice continuing.
cultural_burning.handling_rule: Fire practice is Quandamooka knowledge. Model the ecological effect; do not depict, name or invent the practice. Route any depiction to docs/CULTURAL-REVIEW.md.

wallum_target_fire_interval_years.basis: A modelling placeholder consistent with serotinous banksia needing time to build a seed store. Not a figure from an island fire management plan.

sheoak_recovery_years_after_fire.basis: Modelling placeholder for the glossy black-cockatoo food consequence.

unburnt_refuge_target_share.basis: Modelling placeholder. Ground-dwelling species need unburnt patches inside any burn mosaic.

what_disturbs_it: large single-event fires that leave no unburnt refuge
fire in peat, which can smoulder and destroy the swamp seed bank
what_helps_it: a patchwork of small cool burns rather than one large hot one
processes.sim_role: The central land-management lever. It should be possible for a player to be too fire-averse and lose the wallum, or too fire-happy and lose the she-oaks, cockatoos and ground mammals. Both failures should be legible.

processes.name: Groundwater, the lakes and the borefield
processes.summary: The island is a sand mass holding a very large freshwater store. Every lake, swamp, spring and acid wetland is connected to it. Water is drawn from bores near each township, and a much larger volume is taken for the mainland supply.
processes.mechanism: Window lakes such as Karboora sit in a hollow that intersects the regional water table, so their level follows the aquifer. Perched lakes such as Bummiera sit above it on a sealed organic layer, so they follow rainfall. Eighteen Mile Swamp and the acid wetlands are water-table expressions. Draw the water table down and the window lakes, the swamp and the frog breeding habitat go first; the perched lakes hardly notice.

figures.note: These figures come from secondary reporting and one of the quoted licence numbers was clearly garbled at source. The Seqwater North Stradbroke Island Drought Response Plan is the document to read; it could not be text-extracted in this pass. Treat all four numbers as placeholders and check before any of them reaches a player.

processes.community_concern: Residents have raised concern about sacred lagoons drying. Whether that is attributable to extraction, drought, or both is contested and this pack takes no position on it.
processes.sim_role: The system that ties the civic water lever to the ecology in a way a player will not expect. Turning up the mainland export should lower window lakes, shrink acid wetland area and hurt the wallum frogs with a lag of seasons, while leaving Brown Lake looking fine. That gap between what looks fine and what is happening is the lesson.
what_helps_it: monitoring bores and published lake levels

processes.name: The Amity Point erosion problem
processes.summary: Amity Point is losing land. This is real, current and serious. It is not ordinary beach erosion: the two drivers are episodic flow slides, sudden underwater collapses of the sand slope, and the southerly migration of the deep Rainbow Channel toward the shore.
processes.status: Declared an erosion-prone area under the Coastal Protection and Management Act 1995. Redland City Council adopted a Shoreline Erosion Management Plan in 2019 and an implementation plan in 2021.
processes.losses: The area has a long history of significant erosion resulting in the loss of Indigenous values, public and private land, and assets.

reference_event.description: About 30 metres of foreshore near Toompany Street affected, with three to four metres of land, including trees, falling into the sea.

works.location: Along the coastline behind public land and private properties at Amity Point
works.note: Length and construction date not captured in this pass.
Designed to be concealed under sand so beach access and appearance are kept. Design and approvals funded.
Recommended in the SEMP. Volumes not captured in this pass.

annual_shoreline_retreat_m.basis: No published rate located. Model as episodic events rather than a steady annual rate, because that is how flow slides actually behave.

flow_slide_event_probability_per_year.basis: Unknown. Needs the university flow slide study.

processes.sim_role: The island's hardest civic and ecological trade-off, and it has real houses attached. It should be modelled as episodic and partly unpredictable: a player who budgets for a steady rate will be caught out, which is exactly what happens in reality. The rock wall option protects assets and costs beach; the buried wall costs more and keeps the beach; retreat is the option nobody wants to say out loud.
what_disturbs_it: channel migration, which no local lever controls
loading the top of the slope with hard structures
what_helps_it: monitoring and survey so events are anticipated
planning that does not put new assets in the erosion-prone strip

processes.name: Ocean dune erosion and accretion
processes.summary: The eastern beaches cut back during storms and east swells and rebuild in calmer weather as spinifex traps windblown sand. The dune is a buffer that spends itself and refills. Whether it refills depends on how much vegetation is left and how many tracks cut through it.

storm_cut_volume_m3_per_m_range.basis: Order of magnitude for a significant east coast storm cut on an exposed sandy beach. Not measured for this island. Replace with survey data if it can be found.

recovery_months_range.basis: Modelling placeholder. Recovery is faster with intact spinifex and slower after repeat storms.

vegetation_cover_multiplier.note: Recovery rate scales with hab-foredune vegetation cover. Cover falls with each unmanaged access track and rises with fencing, matting, sand ladders and planting.

management_options.option: One well-made access corridor per beach instead of many goat tracks
management_options.effect: Concentrates trampling, lets the rest of the dune recover.

management_options.option: Sand ladder and matting on worn accesses
management_options.effect: Stops the dune bleeding out through the gap.
Closes a storm gap before wind widens it.
Gives the dune a firmer base for the season.

processes.sim_role: A slow variable the player can only manage through small, cheap, unglamorous actions. It should be possible to lose a dune over ten sim years without ever making a single visibly bad decision.
what_disturbs_it: storm sequences with no recovery gap
hard structures that reflect wave energy and scour the sand in front of them

processes.name: Shorebird roost disturbance
processes.summary: Migratory shorebirds feed on the exposed flats and roost above the tide line at high water. Every time a roost is flushed, a bird spends energy it needs for a flight to the northern hemisphere. Disturbance is cumulative and mostly invisible to the person causing it.

drone_exclusion_radius_m.basis: Recommended in the literature for waterbird flocks likely to contain eastern curlews.

sim_parameters.roost_window: High tide, when the feeding flats are covered.

energy_cost_per_flush.basis: Mechanism is well established; a per-flush energy figure was not located. Model as a proportion of the daily budget and calibrate against the departure-weight requirement.

processes.sim_role: The mechanic that teaches cumulative harm. No single dog walk matters. Forty of them in a summer does. The player sees no dead birds, only a number falling, which is exactly the honest problem.
what_disturbs_it: people walking through a roost to get a photo
loss of roost sites to development and rising sea level

the_instruments_over_it.note: Disturbing a roost is a local act with an international audience, and the honest part is that none of these instruments makes it an offence. Every one of them obliges a government to try, to cooperate or to report. The only rung that reaches a person standing on the sand is the Australian statute at the end of the chain, and even that turns on whether an action is likely to have a significant impact, which is a judgement this project does not make.
the_instruments_over_it.site: Moreton Bay, Ramsar site 631, designated 22 October 1993, official area 120,639 ha. The site meets all nine criteria for designation as a Wetland of International Importance.
the_instruments_over_it.site_holds: More than 50,000 waterbirds, at least 43 species of shorebird and at least 28 migratory shorebird species. Migratory shorebirds were estimated at 33,929 individuals over 2013 to 2017, counted by the Queensland Wader Study Group at no fewer than 40 high tide roost sites.
the_instruments_over_it.the_island_in_the_line: The 2018 boundary description takes the site in along the western side of Minjerribah through fish habitat area FHA-017, Myora to Amity Banks, and takes in Myora Conservation Park and two remnant patches in the south. It excludes freehold and four named exclusion areas at Dunwich, Point Lookout, Amity Point and the southern end. The line runs around the townships and takes in the flats.
the_instruments_over_it.flyway_network_site: EAAF013. There are no legally binding implications for a Flyway Network Site at national or Queensland level, and an owner or manager is not required to alter a land use or produce a plan because of it.
the_instruments_over_it.civic_ref: data/civic.json treaty_layer, where each of these carries what it obliges, whom it binds and what it does not do

processes.name: Seagrass condition on the Eastern Banks
processes.summary: The banks off the island's western side carry the meadows that hold the dugong and the turtles. Species composition shifts over time: Oceana serrulata has increased at Amity and Wanga-Wallen Banks, replacing Zostera muelleri as the dominant.

flood_plume_impact.note: Turbidity after major catchment flooding is the main external shock. This is a mainland catchment problem the island cannot fix, which is worth making explicit to the player.

dugong_grazing_recovery.note: Grazing removes most of the shoot density and biomass in a patch, then the herd moves on and the patch regrows. Model as a rotating disturbance with recovery, not as loss.

processes.sim_role: Slow marine variable driving dugong and green turtle numbers. Its main driver is off-island, which is a useful limit on player agency.
what_disturbs_it: boat propeller scarring in shallow water

processes.name: Feral predator control
processes.summary: Sustained fox and cat control across the island, run in partnership by QYAC, Queensland Parks, Council, Seqwater, Sibelco, Healthy Land & Water and state agencies. Baiting since 2017 as part of more than a decade of work. About 90 per cent of foxes removed. The last recorded turtle nest predation was in late 2016.

lapse_penalty.note: Model recovery of the fox population as fast relative to the removal effort. A one-year budget gap should not simply pause the gains, it should give some of them back.

processes.sim_role: The best argument in the pack for recurrent funding over capital funding. The fox line item is small, boring, and the thing most likely to be cut in a tight budget round. Cutting it should cost the player turtle hatchlings, bandicoots and ground-nesting birds within a few seasons.

processes.name: Whale season
processes.summary: Humpbacks pass close inshore at Point Lookout twice a year: north roughly June to August, south roughly September to November. Deep water near the headland means the whole thing can be watched from land.
processes.sim_role: Couples ecology to the visitor economy. Whale season fills the ferry, the accommodation and the headland car park, which then raises shorebird disturbance, parking pressure, waste volume and wildlife call volume. Do not model it as scenery.
what_disturbs_it: entanglement in fishing and shark control gear

processes.name: Wildlife rescue response
processes.summary: Live rescue on the island runs through Wildlife Rescue Minjerribah, with the Queensland marine stranding hotline for turtles, dolphins, whales and dugongs. The public is never asked to rescue, handle, contain or touch an animal.

contacts.name: Wildlife Rescue Minjerribah
contacts.when: First call for everything on the island

contacts.name: Triple Zero
contacts.when: Any person in danger, snake bite, bat scratch or bite

commonest_cases: fishing gear on seabirds and pelicans, the island's commonest bird call
koala on the ground or hit on the road
kangaroo or wallaby hit, with a joey possibly alive in the pouch
cat-caught possum or bird, urgent even when it looks unhurt
processes.sim_role: The player-facing feedback loop for every negative wildlife event. A rescue system that is legible and correct is more valuable here than a detailed one: the rules above are the same rules a real caller is given.
processes.source_note: The triage tree in that repo is a draft for Wildlife Rescue Minjerribah to review. Treat its wording as provisional and do not present it as the team's approved script.

seasonal_calendar.label: Summer
ecology: Loggerhead turtle nesting and hatching on the ocean beaches
Manta rays on the bommie
Migratory shorebirds at peak numbers on the western flats
Acid frogs calling after storm rain
Goannas visible around campgrounds
Cane toad breeding
Peak visitor pressure on every one of the above

seasonal_calendar.label: Autumn
ecology: Shorebirds fatten and depart for the northern hemisphere by about April
Midyim fruiting ends
Fox control season begins about April
Planned burn season opens
Mullet start moving

seasonal_calendar.label: Winter
ecology: Humpbacks passing north, peaking about July
The mullet run, May to August
Tailor in the gutters, strong in August
Grey nurse sharks aggregating at Flat Rock, June to October
Echidna breeding, with a road strike peak
Wallum froglet calling
Banksia and swamp mahogany flowering, feeding gliders and flying-foxes
Sea-eagle and osprey nesting
Planned burns

seasonal_calendar.label: Spring
ecology: Humpbacks passing south with calves, close inshore, peaking about October
Snakes and blue-tongues at their most active and most reported
Rainbow bee-eaters back and digging nest burrows in sandy banks
Koala breeding and dispersal, with a road strike and dog attack peak
Shorebirds returning from about September
Loggerhead mating from late October
Bushfire risk rising

guidance: Populations here move on a scale of seasons and years, not ticks. Anything that changes visibly within one in-game day is probably wrong.

Most population_estimate values in this pack are null on purpose. Use the habitat area and a density parameter, and expose the density as a tunable so a local can correct it, rather than hard-coding a headline number nobody can source.
Where a figure is for Moreton Bay rather than the island, it says so. Do not present a bay-wide count as an island count.
Never call Math.random. Use world.rng.stream for anything stochastic, including fire ignition, flow slide events and storm cuts.
The three predator pressures (fox, cat, roaming dog) should share one control-effort budget so the player feels the trade-off between them.
sim_defaults.indicator_rationale: Seven species that between them read the road network, the aquifer, visitor behaviour, the fox budget, the fire interval, the seagrass and the whole predator system. If a player can only watch seven numbers, these are the seven.
